summary: Defines an IMAP4 extension for non-synchronizing literals, so a client can send large pieces of data without waiting for the server's go-ahead each time. It was replaced by RFC 7888.

plainLanguage.summary: This IMAP extension removes a wait before the client sends a literal string. The client can use it only when the server advertises support.

questions: what is a non-synchronizing literal in imap
how does imap literal plus save a round trip
what is an imap non-synchronizing literal
what does the imap literal plus sign mean
subtitle: An IMAP literal form that lets a client send data without waiting for a continuation request.

tldr.problem: With a synchronizing IMAP literal, the client waits for the server's continuation request after sending the octet count and before sending the string.
tldr.mechanism: A non-synchronizing literal adds a plus sign before the closing brace. The client can send its data immediately when the server advertises the LITERAL+ capability.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2088 was obsoleted by RFC 7888 and updated by RFC 4466.

today: RFC 2088 is obsoleted by RFC 7888 and updated by RFC 4466, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Extra Round Trip
sections.content:
IMAP4 uses literals to communicate strings. In the normal client-to-server form, the client sends the octet count and waits for a command continuation request before sending the string data.

RFC 2088 defines an alternative that avoids this wait. It calls the original form a synchronizing literal and the new form a non-synchronizing literal.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual literal form makes the client pause for the server's signal before sending the string. This extension allows the client to continue without that pause.

sections.title: The Plus-Sign Form
sections.content:
A non-synchronizing literal is marked with a plus sign between the octet count and closing brace, as in {11+}. The server does not send a continuation request, and the client does not need to wait before sending the stated number of octets.

A client may use the form only if the server advertises LITERAL+ in its CAPABILITY response. Otherwise, it must use synchronizing literals. The server must detect the marker at the end of a line and treat the specified following octets and line as part of the same command.
sections.plainLanguage: The plus sign tells the server that the literal data follows right away. The client first checks that the server announced LITERAL+ support.

sections.title: Example and Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC shows a LOGIN command in which the client sends literals for the user name and password without waiting for continuation requests between them. The server then returns a tagged successful completion.

The formal syntax allows an optional plus sign inside the literal marker. The RFC reports no known security issues with the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The example sends both login strings consecutively. A server that supports the extension does not ask for a separate go-ahead between them.
